cells.tense: You are bearing a beginning steady, and the bearing is not hurting it.
cells.ask: Give the support you've been giving quietly one plain name, out loud, to whoever receives it. Then let it be enough for today. No follow-up expected.
cells.core:
You've got a start in your hands and you're not crushing it. It's early, barely anything to show, and you can carry that without bracing, without rushing to prove it's real. People around you get steadier when you're near, and mostly you don't notice you're doing it. Staying power is its own kind of work, and it's going fine.

The one thing to watch: strength handed out everywhere can leave the rest of you unaccounted for. Support goes two ways, or it thins. Tell one person what you're actually carrying, and let some of it flow back. You don't have to bear everything alone to bear it well.
cells.sheetLine: You hold beginnings without breaking them. Say where it goes.
cells.place: the staying power that keeps a beginning unbroken

cells.tense: You are already bearing the weight of how this ends, before it has started.
cells.ask: Pick the smallest next piece and do only that one. When you finish it, stop for the day and don't plan the rest. Let the plan catch up to you.
cells.core:
You're holding the whole shape of this before it's even started. Every way it could fall apart, every load it'll put on you, you've taken on ahead of time, and now your arms are full of something that hasn't happened. Bracing feels like getting ready. It's costing you the beginning you actually have.

Going well, you stay in the day you're in. You pick up the weight in front of you, you set it down when the day ends, and you don't carry tomorrow's load tonight. One day's weight is a load you can actually hold. Carry that, and keep your footing.
cells.sheetLine: You're carrying the whole ending before the start.
cells.place: the staying power that keeps a beginning unbroken

cells.tense: You were bearing something real back there, and you've not picked it up since.
cells.ask: Look at the last thing you began, one clear look, no verdict. Name what it actually needs next from you, say it out loud, and then let it wait until you mean it.
cells.core:
Going well looks like this: you pick something up, you stay with it while it's heavy, and you keep your footing without going rigid. That's still yours to do. What happened instead is the setting down. There was a beginning, it weighed something, and you stopped, not decided, just stopped. The staying power didn't leave; it's been running on empty so long it looks like your nature.

What you'd need isn't the will to bear it. It's seeing what's really in your hands, plainly, without flinching. Don't try to feel strong first. That's backwards. Look until it's clear, and the strength shows up because you know what you're looking at. One clear-seeing act, once. Not to prove anything.
cells.sheetLine: You set it down and called that your limit. Look again.
cells.place: the staying power that keeps a beginning unbroken

cells.tense: You are keeping a beginning alive right now, and calling it nothing you're doing.
cells.ask: Finish the sentence 'I'm the one keeping __ going', out loud, alone. Then write down the next step you're already planning. Keep it private if you like.
cells.core:
You keep carrying something that wants to start, and you talk as if it's just the situation. It's not the right time. Things are heavy. But in the moment you choose to keep it going, you spare the thing that would end it, you make room for it, and that's you. Not the circumstances. You've been doing it long enough it feels like the way things are.

The strength is real and running. Only the owning of it is missing. Find the simplest honest version, not the grand one, and say it's yours. When you stop calling it the situation, you get to decide what happens to it.
cells.sheetLine: You're already keeping this alive. You call it staying afloat.
cells.place: the staying power that keeps a beginning unbroken

attempts.check: Unsupported: that a seed being held in Fortitude means a project has already begun or that its beginning is at risk. What a reader might fairly say is different: sometimes the seed is simply waiting, and holding it is the whole job until it's not. If the read is wrong about which part is pressing, the asks still work — each one attaches to something true today. The sentence serving the writer more than the person: 'admit one more thing you keep the roof up with', which is a line I'd enjoy more than a reader would; cut it.
